Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

With that in mind, let's check each function:

- For the first function, we have 

$$
{f}_{1}(x,t)={t}^{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(tx).
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in R$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=2tx\operatorname{cos}⁡(tx)-{t}^{2}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(tx)
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{1}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t.$

- For the second function, we have 

$$
{f}_{2}(x,t)=\frac{1}{(x-t)^{2}+1}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in R$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R$ because the denominator is always positive. Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=\frac{2(x-t)}{{((x-t)^{2}+1)}^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in R.$

- For the third function, we have 

$$
{f}_{3}(x,t)=\frac{x}{x-t}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}<0$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(-\infty ,0)$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that for $t<0$ and $x\in [0,1],$ the denominator $x-t$ is positive, so ${f}_{3}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=\frac{x}{(x-t)^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all $t<0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

Suppose f(x,t) is continuous on R=[a,b]×[c,d] and ∂f∂t exists and is continuous on R. Then, the function F(t)=∫abf(x,t)dx is differentiable on (c,d), and F′(t)=ddt∫abf(x,t)dx=∫ab∂f∂t(x,t)dx. This is known as differentiating under the integral sign.

With that in mind, let's check each function:

  • For the first function, we have f1(x,t)=t2xcos⁡(tx). We fix t0∈R and choose c<t0<d, so R=[0,1]×[c,d].

    Note that f1 is continuous on R. Computing the partial derivative, we have ∂f1∂t=2txcos⁡(tx)−t2x2sin⁡(tx) which exists and is continuous on R. Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at t0. And since our choice of t0 was arbitrary, we can compute F1′(t) for all real t.

  • For the second function, we have f2(x,t)=1(x−t)2+1. We fix t0∈R and choose c<t0<d, so R=[0,1]×[c,d].

    Note that f2 is continuous on R because the denominator is always positive. Computing the partial derivative, we have ∂f2∂t=2(x−t)((x−t)2+1)2 which exists and is continuous on R. Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at t0. And since our choice of t0 was arbitrary, we can compute F2′(t) for all t∈R.

  • For the third function, we have f3(x,t)=xx−t. We fix t0<0 and choose [c,d]⊂(−∞,0) such that c<t0<d, so R=[0,1]×[c,d].

    Note that for t<0 and x∈[0,1], the denominator x−t is positive, so f3 is continuous on R. Computing the partial derivative, we have ∂f3∂t=x(x−t)2 which exists and is continuous on R. Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at t0. And since our choice of t0 was arbitrary, we can compute F3′(t) for all t<0.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."
